issues.legal_issue: Conduct does not estop a person from asserting a property right when it did not induce a mistaken belief or a detrimental change of position.
material_facts: A co-heir claimed possession of her inherited share of property held by her father.

She did not respond to a notice asking her to join a possession suit, wrote that she had no desire to claim the property and that her father could deal with it, and attested a will purporting to dispose of the property.
The father knew the true state of title, and no detrimental change of position by him was shown to have resulted from her conduct.
The will could take effect only on the father's death, so no interest in the property had accrued to the other beneficiaries by the time of the suit.
issues.conclusion: The co-heir was not estopped from claiming possession of her share.
issues.legal_principle: Section 115 of the Evidence Act embodies estoppel by representation. The principle described in Pickard v. Sears, Ganges Manufacturing Co. v. Saurjmull, Cairncross v. Lorimer, Carr v. London & N.W. Ry. Co., and Sarad v. Gopal requires a representation or conduct that induces belief and action to the detriment of the person relying on it. A person who knows the true facts is not misled by a representation. The Court expressed doubt, but did not decide, whether a court may travel beyond section 115 to apply equitable estoppel.

rule.if: property_title_or_possession_dispute and alleged_representation_or_acquiescence and (relying_party_knew_true_facts or no_detrimental_change_of_position)

predicates.property_title_or_possession_dispute: The dispute concerns a person's asserted right to title or possession of property.
predicates.alleged_representation_or_acquiescence: A party relies on another person's words, conduct, silence, or acquiescence as a representation about the property right.
predicates.relying_party_knew_true_facts: The person said to have relied on the representation knew the true state of the relevant facts.
predicates.no_detrimental_change_of_position: The person said to have relied on the representation did not alter their position to their detriment because of it.

issues.definition: When a property-right dispute involves alleged representational conduct, estoppel is not established if the alleged relying party knew the true facts or did not detrimentally change position because of that conduct.

issues.legal_issue: A person who knowingly improves property without the true owner's consent cannot require the owner to pay for those improvements.
material_facts: The father possessed and improved property belonging to his daughters after their mother's death.
He knew, according to the position ultimately established, that the property belonged to the daughters, but dealt with it as he chose.
The improvements were not made with the consent of the co-heir whose share was claimed.
The father and those claiming through him sought to make the co-heir bear a proportionate share of the improvement costs.
issues.conclusion: The co-heir was not liable to pay any part of the alleged improvement costs.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle that a person who knowingly lacks title and spends money improving property cannot charge the true owner for improvements made without that owner's consent. The claim under section 51 of the Transfer of Property Act and reliance on acquiescence did not assist the improver; Ramsden v. Dyson was distinguished.

predicates.property_possession_dispute: The dispute concerns possession of property claimed by its true owner.
predicates.improver_knew_lacked_title: The person who made the improvements knew that they had no title to the property.
predicates.improvements_made_without_owner_consent: The improvements were made without the consent of the person entitled to the property.

issues.definition: If a person knowingly lacking title improves property without the true owner's consent in a property-possession dispute, the owner is not liable for those improvements.

issues.legal_issue: A decree in favour of a defendant who was not formally transposed as a plaintiff is not set aside for that technical defect when the parties claim under the same title and the defendant's claim has been adjudicated.
material_facts: The plaintiff and a co-defendant claimed their respective shares under the same title.
The co-defendant admitted the plaintiff's claim and sought a decree for her own share against the remaining defendants.
The remaining defendants raised special defences against the co-defendant, and the High Court considered and adjudicated those defences before granting her relief.
The co-defendant had not been formally transposed as a plaintiff.
issues.conclusion: The absence of formal transposition did not justify interfering with the decree in the co-defendant's favour.
issues.legal_principle: Order I, rule 10(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure permits a court to transpose a party as a plaintiff, including on the court's own initiative; Bhupender v. Rajeshwar states that this power should be exercised to do complete justice. Order XLI, rule 33 was also relevant to the appellate court's power. Section 99 of the Code barred interference with the decree on this technical ground where the claim had been fully adjudicated.

predicates.appeal_against_decree_for_nontransposed_: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a decree granted to a defendant who was not formally made a plaintiff.
predicates.parties_claim_under_same_title: The plaintiff and the defendant seeking relief claim their rights under the same title.
predicates.defendant_claim_fully_adjudicated: The court considered and decided the defences and merits of the non-transposed defendant's claim.

issues.definition: In an appeal against relief granted to a non-transposed defendant, a decree stands despite the technical defect when the parties claim under the same title and the defendant's claim was fully adjudicated.

issues.legal_issue: Future mesne profits may be awarded to a defendant who substantially seeks the same relief as a plaintiff claiming possession and mesne profits, even if the defendant was not formally transposed as a plaintiff.
material_facts: The plaintiff's suit sought partition and separate possession of her share, as well as mesne profits.
The co-defendant admitted the plaintiff's claim and, in substance, sought a similar decree for her own share.
The High Court awarded the co-defendant future mesne profits along with possession of her share.
The co-defendant had not been formally transposed as a plaintiff.
issues.conclusion: The award of future mesne profits to the co-defendant was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Order XX, rule 12 of the Code of Civil Procedure governs future mesne profits in a suit for recovery of possession of immovable property and rent or mesne profits. The Court distinguished Mohd. Amin v. Vakil Ahmed, where the plaintiffs had not claimed mesne profits, and noted that the plaintiff in this case had claimed them and the co-defendant substantially sought a similar decree. The Court stated that past mesne profits cannot be awarded unless claimed, and left open whether the broader rule concerning future mesne profits required reconsideration.

predicates.possession_or_partition_suit_includes_me: The proceeding seeks possession or partition of property and includes a claim for mesne profits.
predicates.co_defendant_admits_plaintiffs_claim: A co-defendant admits the plaintiff's claim to the relevant property right.
predicates.co_defendant_substantially_seeks_same_re: The co-defendant substantially seeks a decree for the same kind of relief in respect of that co-defendant's own share.

issues.definition: When a possession or partition suit includes a mesne-profits claim and a co-defendant admits the plaintiff's claim while substantially seeking the same relief, future mesne profits may be awarded to that co-defendant.
